reading.identification: A c.16th–17th-century Flemish Renaissance quay house on Korenlei, Ghent — a very narrow gable-fronted canal house in brick with sandstone dressings and a crowned ornamental gable, heavily restored around 1900, now a bar/restaurant at ground level with lettable rooms above.
reading.notes:
STOREYS: set B shows ground (café, largely masked by parasols) + 2 full upper storeys with cross-windows and flower boxes, then a gable containing two further window levels. I read the gable levels as attic, so count=3. 3.8 + 2x3.3 = 10.4 m to eaves leaves ~4.7 m of gable to reach the data height of 15.1 m, which matches the two-tier crowned gable in the photos. Do not "fix" this by adding a storey — a 4th storey would squeeze the gable to under 3 m and contradict what set B shows.

ROOF: marked inferred, not seen, on purpose. The gable SHAPE is genuinely seen (both set B frames show it clear against sky: stepped shoulders with scrolled/voluted transitions and a crowning aedicule with pinnacles). ridge_parallel_to_street=false is inferred from the gable facing the quay; set A is too degraded to confirm a ridge. stepped_gable is the closest enum member — the true profile is a stepped gable with Renaissance scroll infill, so if the generator can bias the step edges toward curved shoulders, do that. Not a bell gable (no smooth klokgevel curve).

FOOTPRINT NOTE: footprint_m [6.3, 3.7] gives a 3.7 m depth, which is far too shallow for this house type and is inconsistent with frontage_width_m 5.4. The polygon is almost certainly a fragment of a deeper party-wall house. I have not contradicted the data, but do not derive roof geometry from that aspect ratio — it would put the ridge parallel to the street, which the street gable rules out.

MATERIAL: wall is orange-red hand-formed brick, weathered, with raked joints — 6 mm RMS carries the 1-10 cm regime; do NOT mesh the brick relief. trim is Balegem-type sandy limestone (the string courses, mullions, sills, gable dressings). "marble" was the only natural-stone enum member but is wrong electrically — dense calcite sits near eps'=7.1 whereas this porous weathered limestone is nearer 5-6, so concrete is the better ITU analogue. Give the trim a lower roughness than the wall (~1.5 mm) if the generator supports per-class roughness; the dressed stone is much smoother than the brick.

GEOMETRY BUDGET (>10 cm, worth explicit facets): the continuous sandstone string courses at every floor line are the dominant horizontal relief on this facade and are the single most important thing to model — they project clearly and run the full frontage. Then the projecting window sills, the stone mullion+transom crosses standing proud of the glazing plane, the deep reveals, and the stepped/scrolled gable profile with its cornice ledges and crowning aedicule. The gable steps are silhouette edges seen from every camera angle — spend there. Flower boxes sit on the sills at every level and are ~30 cm deep; they are real occluders and belong as geometry, not texture.

NO BALCONIES. The flower boxes are not balconies and must not be promoted into them.

CLUTTER / STREET: fronting street is Korenlei, highway=pedestrian, car_access=none. ZERO vehicles. Do not park anything here — this is exactly the case the parked-car rule got wrong. What does belong, at 7.7 m from the facade: a dense café terrace (large black square parasols, rattan/bistro chairs, small round tables, patio heaters, a barrel table, an A-board menu, planters), moored boats and a quay edge with bollards and railing on the canal side, wall-mounted lanterns and a projecting sign bracket at ground floor. The terrace furniture is the near-field clutter that will actually dominate street-level scattering here, more than the facade relief does.

BUDGET: this facade is 7.7 m from the corridor and the frontage is only 5.4 m wide, so it is cheap to detail well. Give it high resolution on the gable silhouette, the openings and the ground-floor café glazing; the rear and party walls are fully occluded by attached_neighbours=2 and deserve nothing.

CONFIDENCE: 0.72. Wall material, window subdivision, sills, string courses and ground-floor use are solid from set B. Residual uncertainty is the storey/attic split, and the fact that the magenta box in set B frame 1 straddles this house and its lighter-stone neighbour, so a small amount of the neighbour's fabric may have leaked into my reading — I keyed the facade description off frame 0, where the box sits cleanly on the brick house.
